comparison: Both strongly support the MS2-based RNA pull-down proteomics approach (C3, C43, C49-C58, C69, C71, C158). OpenEval emphasizes technical validation with known interactors and appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'enrichment of a set of proteins on FMR1-polyG RNA' and state authors 'provide solid evidence' for identifying RAN translation factors.

Both support RPS26 depletion effects on FMRpolyG translation (C59-C62, C70, C96-C99). OpenEval highlights multiple reporter systems and dose-response data. Peer reviewers confirm 'siRNA depletion of ribosomal protein RPS26 results in less production of FMR1polyG' and note experiments across multiple cell lines increase confidence.

Both support toxicity reduction data (C63-C65, C73, C161). OpenEval details microscopy quantification and apoptosis assays with statistical analysis. Peer reviewers acknowledge the toxicity findings without concerns, confirming RPS26 knockdown affects polyG levels and associated phenotypes.

Both support the selective effect on FMRpolyG versus FMRP translation (C96-C99, C104-C105, overlapping with C46-C47, C102-C103, C129, C170, C210). OpenEval emphasizes this selectivity as mechanistically important. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'approximately 80% of proteins, including FMRP, were not influenced' by RPS26 depletion.

Both support that global translation is maintained despite RPS26 depletion (C83-C84, C137, C193-C194). OpenEval highlights SUnSET assay with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly state RPS26 knockdown 'surprisingly did not strongly affect global translation, as assessed by puromycin incorporation' and note improved data increases confidence.

Both support the SILAC-MS proteomic analysis findings (C107-C117, C169). OpenEval details high identification confidence and statistical rigor. Peer reviewers acknowledge the quantitative mass spectrometry showing selective protein sensitivity to RPS26 depletion while most proteins remain unaffected.

OpenEval supports codon substitution and ASO experiments (C118-C121, C128) as providing direct evidence for ACG codon-specific effects. However, Peer Reviewer 3 expresses uncertainty, stating 'results of the ASO-based ACG codon-blocking experiment in Figure 4G are difficult to interpret' and suggests ASO treatment may interfere with ribosomal scanning rather than demonstrating ACG-codon selection.

Both support TSR2 experiments phenocopying RPS26 depletion (C130-C136, C141, C173-C174, C176). OpenEval notes selective effects mirror RPS26 results but mechanism remains unclear. Peer reviewers accept the findings without specific concerns, consistent with their acceptance of RPS26 data.

Both support the RPS6 negative control experiment (C138-C140). OpenEval emphasizes this establishes specificity and differential proliferation effects. Peer reviewers accept this control without concerns, strengthening the specificity argument for RPS26's role.

Both support RPS25 experiments extending findings to another 40S protein (C142-C149). OpenEval notes relevance of neuronal cell testing and RNA interaction confirmation. Peer reviewers accept the findings as consistent with RPS26 results, part of 'solid evidence' for factors mediating RAN translation.

Both support biochemical validation of RPS26-RNA interaction (C66-C68). OpenEval highlights orthogonal confirmation via biotinylated RNA pull-downs. Peer reviewers accept this validation without concerns as supporting the mass spectrometry findings.

Both support the characterization of stable cell models (C85-C95). OpenEval details microscopy, western blot, and RT-qPCR validation. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'experiments were performed in several cell lines and with several reporters' as a strength increasing confidence.

Both support validation with known RPS26 responders (C100-C101). OpenEval notes this confirms siRNA efficacy. Peer reviewers accept this validation control without concerns as strengthening confidence in RPS26 knockdown experiments.

Both support cell proliferation effects without increased cell death (C80-C82, overlapping with C84). OpenEval provides quantitative data from cell counting and viability assays. Peer reviewers acknowledge RPS26 knockdown 'led to decreases in cell growth' while accepting global translation is maintained.

Both support bioinformatic characterization of RPS26-sensitive transcripts (C115-C117, C122-C126, C204-C206). OpenEval details comprehensive analysis identifying GC-richness and sequence features. Peer reviewers accept this characterization without concerns as part of overall findings.

Both support GO analysis and validation of proteomic hits (C112-C114). OpenEval notes logical enrichment of translation-related proteins and reasonable validation rate. Peer reviewers accept the proteomic characterization as part of the SILAC-MS findings.

Both address the -4 position mutagenesis experiment (C118). OpenEval supports this as showing no effect, contrasting with yeast data and suggesting species-specific differences. Peer reviewers do not specifically critique this negative result.

Both support background claims about fragile X-associated conditions and established knowledge (C1-C2, C9-C35, C40-C42, C150-C152, overlapping with extensive background claims). OpenEval notes well-established, appropriately cited literature. Peer reviewers implicitly accept background by not challenging it and noting broad interest across disciplines.

Both support background knowledge about RPS26 function and related biology (C36-C39, C44, C74-C79, C162-C168, C171, C190-C192, C199-C203). OpenEval notes well-cited contextual information. Peer reviewers accept the literature review and contextual framing without challenge.

Both support literature review on RAN translation regulation (C153-C157, C207-C208). OpenEval notes accurate, appropriately cited review justifying the study. Peer reviewers accept the background literature without concerns.

Both support observations about ribosomal composition changes (C181, C185). OpenEval notes these findings support the mechanism and are consistent with ribosome heterogeneity literature. Peer reviewers accept these observations without concerns.

OpenEval marks mechanistic interpretations as uncertain/speculative (C106, C127, C195), noting lack of CGG repeat length dependence is well-supported but mechanistic basis requires investigation. Peer reviewers express similar uncertainty, explicitly stating 'the mechanism by which RPS26 depletion affects translation is still unclear' and questioning whether data 'fully support the authors' critical conclusions.'

OpenEval supports main conclusions about RPS26's selective role in RAN translation (C8, C47, C72, C129, C160, C170, C209-C211) but notes therapeutic potential is speculative. Peer reviewers support the core selectivity findings (C46-C47, C102-C105, C129, C170, C210) as part of 'solid evidence' for RPS26's role.

OpenEval supports main conclusions (C8, C47, C72, C129, C160, C170, C209-C211) with caveat about therapeutic speculation. Peer reviewers (R18) express uncertainty about mechanistic claims (C4-C8, C48, C106, C127, C159-C160, C175, C178, C188, C195, C209, C211), noting mechanism remains unclear and requesting additional validation.

Both support broader implications and connections to RPS26 roles in other diseases (C179-C180, C182-C184, C186-C187, C189). OpenEval notes FXPOI connection is speculative but reasonable. Peer reviewers accept the discussion of broader implications as part of contextual framing.
